title: First healing, then the mysteries
source_text: Εἶτα μετὰ ταῦτα αἰσθόμενος ἑαυτοῦ ὁ Κέλσος πικρότερον ἡμῖν λοιδορησαμένου ὡσπερεὶ ἀπολογούμενος τοιαῦτά φησιν· ὅτι δὲ οὐδὲν πικρότερον ἐπαιτιῶμαι ἢ ἐφ᾿ ὅσον ἡ ἀλήθεια βιάζεται, τεκμαιρέσθω καὶ τοῖσδέ τις, οἱ μὲν γὰρ εἰς τὰς ἄλλας τελετὰς καλοῦντες προκηρύττουσι τάδε· ὅστις χεῖρας καθαρὸς καὶ φωνὴν συνετὸς, καὶ αὖθις ἕτεροι· ὅστις ἁγνὸς ἀπὸ παντὸς μύσους, καὶ ὅτῳ ἡ ψυχὴ οὐδὲν σύνοιδε κακὸν, καὶ ὅτῳ εὖ καὶ δικαίως βεβίωται, καὶ ταῦτα προκηρύττουσιν οἱ καθάρσια ἁμαρτημάτων ὑπισχνούμενοι, ἐπακούσωμεν δὲ τίνας ποτὲ οὗτοι καλοῦσιν· ὅστις, φασὶν, ἁμαρτωλὸς, ὅστις ἀσύνετος, ὅστις νήπιος, καὶ ὡς ἁπλῶς εἰπεῖν ὅστις κακοδαίμων, τοῦτον ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ δέξεται, τὸν ἁμαρτωλὸν ἆρα οὐ τοῦτον λέγετε, τὸν ἄδικον καὶ κλέπτην καὶ τοιχωρύχον καὶ φαρμακέα καὶ ἱερόσυλον καὶ τυμβωρύχον; τίνας ἂν ἄλλους προκηρύττων λῃστὴς ἐκάλεσε; καὶ πρὸς ταῦτα δέ φαμεν οτι οὐ ταὐτόν ἐστι νοσοῦντας τὴν ψυχὴν ἐπὶ θεραπείαν καλεῖν καὶ ὑγιαίνοντας ἐπὶ τὴν τῶν θειοτέρων γνῶσιν καὶ ἐπιστήμην, καὶ ἡμεῖς δὲ ἀμφότερα ταῦτα γινώσκοντες, κατ᾿ ἀρχὰς μὲν προκαλούμενοι ἐπὶ τὸ θεραπευθῆναι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους προτρέπομεν τοὺς ἁμαρτωλοὺς ἥκειν ἐπὶ τοὺς διδάσκοντας λόγους μὴ ἁμαρτάνειν καὶ τοὺς ἀσυνέτους ἐπὶ τοὺς ἐμποιοῦντας σύνεσιν καὶ τοὺς νηπίους εἰς τὸ ἀναβαίνειν φρονήματι ἐπὶ τὸν ἄνδρα καὶ τοὺς ἁπλῶς κακοδαίμονας ἐπὶ εὐδαιμονίαν ἢ, ὅπερ κυριώτερόν ἐστιν εἰπεῖν, ἐπὶ μακαριότητα, ἐπὰν δ᾿ οἱ προκόπτοντες τῶν προτραπέντων παραστήσωσι τὸ κεκαθάρθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου καὶ ὅση δύναμις βέλτιον βεβιωκέναι, τὸ τηνικάδε καλοῦμεν αὐτοὺς ἐπὶ τὰς παρ᾿ ἡμῖν τελετάς· „σοφίαν γὰρ λαλοῦμεν ἐν τοῖς τελείοις“.
pass_a_gloss: Then after these, Celsus, perceiving himself having abused (λοιδορέω) us more bitterly, as if (ὡσπερεί) defending himself, says such things: [Celsus] That I accuse nothing more bitterly than so far as the truth (ἀλήθεια) compels (βιάζομαι), let one judge also from these. For those calling to the other rites (τελετή) proclaim beforehand (προκηρύττω) these: whoever [is] pure (καθαρός) of hands and intelligent (συνετός) of voice (φωνή); and again others: whoever [is] holy/pure (ἁγνός) from every defilement (μύσος), and whose soul is conscious (σύνοιδα) of nothing evil, and by whom it has been lived (βιόω) well and justly (δικαίως). And these proclaim those promising purifications (καθάρσια) of sins (ἁμάρτημα). But let us listen (ἐπακούω) whom these call: whoever, they say, [is] a sinner (ἁμαρτωλός), whoever without understanding (ἀσύνετος), whoever a child (νήπιος), and simply (ἁπλῶς) to say, whoever wretched (κακοδαίμων), this one the kingdom (βασιλεία) of God will receive (δέχομαι). The sinner — do you not say this one, the unjust (ἄδικος) and thief (κλέπτης) and housebreaker (τοιχωρύχος) and poisoner/sorcerer (φαρμακεύς) and temple-robber (ἱερόσυλος) and grave-robber (τυμβωρύχος)? Whom else would a robber (λῃστής) proclaiming have called? [Origen] And to these we say that it is not the same to call those sick (νοσέω) in soul to healing (θεραπεία) and the healthy (ὑγιαίνω) to knowledge (γνῶσις) and understanding (ἐπιστήμη) of more divine things (θειότερα). And we, knowing both of these, at the beginnings (κατ᾿ ἀρχάς), calling people to be healed (θεραπεύω), urge (προτρέπω) the sinners to come to the words (λόγοι) teaching not to sin, and those without understanding to those producing (ἐμποιέω) understanding (σύνεσις), and the children to go up (ἀναβαίνω) in mind (φρόνημα) to the man (ἀνήρ), and the simply wretched to happiness (εὐδαιμονία) or, what is more proper (κυριώτερον) to say, to blessedness (μακαριότης). But when those making progress (προκόπτω) of those urged present (παρίστημι) that they have been purified (καθαίρω) by the Word (λόγος) and as far as possible have lived better, then we call them to the rites (τελετή) among us: for we speak (λαλέω) wisdom (σοφία) among the perfect (τέλειος).
pass_b_english: Then after this Celsus, aware that he has abused us rather too bitterly, says, as though defending himself: “That I am making no harsher accusation than the truth compels, let anyone judge from the following as well. Those who summon people to the other rites of initiation proclaim beforehand: ‘Whoever has clean hands and intelligent speech’; and others again: ‘Whoever is pure from every defilement, whose soul is conscious of no evil, and who has lived well and justly.’ These are the proclamations of those who promise purification from sins. But let us hear whom these people summon. ‘Whoever is a sinner,’ they say, ‘whoever is without understanding, whoever is a child, and, in a word, whoever is wretched, him the kingdom of God will receive.’ Do you not mean by ‘the sinner’ the unjust man, the thief, the housebreaker, the poisoner, the temple-robber and the grave-robber? Whom else would a robber summon by public proclamation?”

To this we reply that it is not the same thing to call those who are sick in soul to healing, and those who are healthy to the knowledge and understanding of diviner things. We know both of these. At the beginning, when we invite people to be healed, we urge sinners to come to the teachings that teach them not to sin, those without understanding to the teachings that produce understanding, children to rise in mind to manhood, and, in a word, the wretched to happiness, or, to use the more proper word, to blessedness. But when those among them who are making progress show that they have been cleansed by the Word and, as far as they can, have lived a better life, then we call them to our own rites of initiation, for “we speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Corinthians 2:6).

choices.choice: Celsus’s words are in double quotation marks; the proclamations he reports, and the Christian invitation he puts in Christian mouths (φασίν), are in single quotation marks inside them. ὅστις χεῖρας καθαρὸς καὶ φωνὴν συνετός is the known form of the Eleusinian proclamation, which excluded those of unintelligible (that is, non-Greek) speech; Origen in 3.60 reinterprets φωνὴν συνετός as understanding speech, so ‘intelligent speech’ is chosen to carry both senses. No classical source citation is added, since the exact source is not certain. The Christian ‘proclamation’ in Celsus is his own caricature, not a quotation; it may echo Matthew 9:13 or Matthew 18:3 and 19:14, but these are not cited inline because the wording is Celsus’s. φαρμακέα: ‘poisoner’ (the word also covers sorcerer). εἰς τὸ ἀναβαίνειν φρονήματι ἐπὶ τὸν ἄνδρα may glance at 1 Corinthians 13:11 or Ephesians 4:13 (εἰς ἄνδρα τέλειον); uncertain, so not cited inline. ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου capitalised ‘the Word’ as Origen’s divine Logos who heals and cleanses (compare 3.61, ἐν τῇ τοῦ λόγου θειότητι); τοὺς διδάσκοντας λόγους are ‘teachings’, lowercase. τέλειοι keeps its play on τελεταί (‘rites’) and Celsus’s τὸ τέλειον in 3.55; rendered ‘perfect’. οτι in the staged text = ὅτι.
τοὺς ἁπλῶς κακοδαίμονας: ‘the simply wretched’ to ‘in a word, the wretched’, echoing Celsus’s ὡς ἁπλῶς εἰπεῖν
οἱ προκόπτοντες τῶν προτραπέντων: ‘those of the persuaded’ (προτρέπω is ‘urge’, not ‘persuade’) to ‘those among them who are making progress’
1 Corinthians 2:6 checked (σοφίαν δὲ λαλοῦμεν ἐν τοῖς τελείοις); Celsus’s words and the proclamations inside them kept in double and single quotation marks
